title: Validity of smartwatch-derived estimates of lactate threshold heart rate and pace compared to graded exercise testing
authors: Lu C, Cui W, Zhu Z, Wu Y, Xing Q, Pan B, Shen Y
population: 100 healthy recreational runners doing indoor graded tests (modified Dmax) then outdoor smartwatch LT tests with Huawei GT Runner (n = 100), Garmin Forerunner 265/265s (n = 23) and Coros Pace3 (n = 17)
findings: LT HR: no significant difference from the lab estimate, but MAE 10.66 bpm (MAPE 6.32%) Huawei, 11.44 bpm (7.15%) Garmin and 8.93 bpm (5.95%) Coros, with r = 0.13 to 0.67 (R2 0.02 to 0.45).

LT pace was overestimated: Huawei MAE 1.22 km/h (MAPE 12.70%, p = 0.01, r = 0.88), Garmin 2.17 km/h (25.78%, p < 0.01, r = 0.73), Coros 1.93 km/h (22.63%, p = 0.08, r = 0.79). The Coros overestimate was not significant by its own p-value despite the abstract's 'all devices' wording.
Authors conclude smartwatches can estimate LT HR and LT pace in recreational runners but tend to overestimate LT pace and accuracy remains to be improved.
limitations: Unequal device groups (Garmin n = 23, Coros n = 17); the reference is lab modified Dmax, not maximal lactate steady state; healthy recreational runners only; closed-source algorithms.
implications: Do not use watch-reported LT pace as a zone anchor without confirmation (race or time-trial result): it overestimated by about 13-26% (MAPE).
Watch LT HR (MAE about 9-11 bpm, weak correlation) is only a rough starting point; allow user override and prefer zones from observed max HR and recent hard efforts.
LT pace correlated with the lab value (r 0.73-0.88) while biased high, so a user-specific correction could be tested, but this paper does not validate one.
